ar: أبو الطيب أحمد بن الحسين المتنبي (303–354 هـ / 915–965 م) أشهر شعراء العربية وأكثرهم حضوراً على الألسنة إلى اليوم. وُلد في الكوفة، وتنقّل صغيراً في بادية الشام، وتقول الروايات إنه سُجن في شبابه بعد أن ادّعى النبوة، ومن هنا جاء لقبه «المتنبي». بلغ ذروة شعره في بلاط سيف الدولة الحمداني في حلب، حيث قال قصائده «السيفيات» في وصف معارك الأمير مع الروم، ثم رحل إلى مصر ومدح كافوراً الإخشيدي قبل أن يهجوه ويفرّ منها.

قُتل في طريق عودته من بلاد فارس قرب دير العاقول على يد فاتك الأسدي. تجمع قصائده بين الحكمة والفخر وقوة العبارة، وكثير من أبياته صار أمثالاً، مثل «على قدر أهل العزم تأتي العزائم». في المكتبة مئات من قصائده من ويكي مصدر، و[شرح ديوانه](/book/1965484) للبرقوقي، ومقالنا [من هو المتنبي ولماذا تُقرأ قصائده اليوم؟](/articles/al-mutanabbi)
ومن أبياته في الثقة بشعره قوله: «وما الدهرُ إلا من رواةِ قصائدي ... إذا قلتُ شعراً أصبحَ الدهرُ منشِدا»، وقد صدق، فما زال الدهر ينشد شعره بعد أكثر من ألف عام.
en: Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi (915–965) is the most quoted poet in Arabic. Born in Kufa, he was jailed as a young man, the story goes, for claiming to be a prophet, which gave him his name ('the would-be prophet'). His finest poems were written at the court of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo, celebrating the prince's wars against Byzantium; he later praised and then satirised Kafur, ruler of Egypt, and was killed on the road near Baghdad in 965.
His lines on ambition, pride and fate became proverbs. The library holds hundreds of his poems from Wikisource and al-Barquqi's [commentary on his diwan](/book/1965484?lang=en).

ar: أبو العلاء أحمد بن عبد الله المعري (363–449 هـ / 973–1057 م) شاعر وفيلسوف من معرة النعمان في الشام، فقد بصره صغيراً بسبب الجدري، ولم يمنعه ذلك من أن يصبح من أوسع علماء عصره معرفة باللغة والشعر. زار بغداد ثم عاد إلى بلدته ولزم بيته قرابة خمسين عاماً، فسمّى نفسه «رهين المحبسين»: العمى والبيت.

من أشهر آثاره ديوان «سقط الزند» من شعر شبابه، و«اللزوميات» التي التزم فيها ما لا يلزم من القافية وبثّ فيها تأملاته في الحياة والموت والناس، و[رسالة الغفران](/book/1965893) التي يتخيل فيها رحلة إلى العالم الآخر يلقى فيها الشعراء والأدباء. في المكتبة عدد كبير من قصائده من ويكي مصدر، فاقرأ منها لتعرف شاعراً سبق عصره في الشك والتأمل.

ومن أبياته المشهورة التي تلخّص نظرته المتشائمة قوله: «هذا جناه أبي عليّ وما جنيتُ على أحد»، ويُروى أنه أوصى أن يُكتب على قبره. ويُعد المعري من أوائل الشعراء العرب الذين جعلوا الشعر وسيلة للتفكير الفلسفي في الوجود والعدل والمصير. وفي المكتبة مئات من قصائده.
en: Abu al-Ala al-Ma'arri (973–1057), the blind poet-philosopher of Ma'arrat al-Nu'man in Syria, lost his sight to smallpox as a child and became one of the most learned men of his time. After a stay in Baghdad he shut himself away at home for almost fifty years, calling himself 'the prisoner of two prisons': blindness and his house.

His youthful diwan Saqt al-Zand, the sceptical, demanding Luzumiyyat and the [Epistle of Forgiveness](/book/1965893?lang=en), an imagined journey to the afterlife among poets, still read as remarkably modern.

ar: جبران خليل جبران (1883–1931) أديب وفنان لبناني، وُلد في بشرّي في جبل لبنان، وهاجر مع أمه وإخوته إلى بوسطن في الولايات المتحدة وهو في الثانية عشرة. كتب بالعربية أولاً، فكانت «الأرواح المتمردة» و[الأجنحة المتكسرة](/book/1966031) التي تُعد من بواكير الرواية العربية، ثم كتب بالإنجليزية أشهر كتبه [النبي](/book/98) (1923)، الذي تُرجم إلى عشرات اللغات وما زال من أكثر الكتب قراءة في العالم.

كان جبران من مؤسسي «الرابطة القلمية» في نيويورك مع ميخائيل نعيمة وإيليا أبو ماضي، وهي الجماعة التي جددت الأدب العربي في المهجر. يجمع أسلوبه بين الشعر والنثر، والتأمل الروحي والتمرد على التقاليد. في المكتبة كتبه بالعربية والإنجليزية، ومنها [المجنون](/book/101).

وكان جبران رساماً أيضاً، درس الفن في باريس، وزيّنت لوحاته ورسومه كتبه، ومنها «النبي» نفسه. توفي في نيويورك عام 1931، ونُقل جثمانه إلى بلدته بشرّي، حيث صار الدير الذي دُفن فيه متحفاً يضم لوحاته ومقتنياته. وتجد في المكتبة كثيراً من كتبه بالعربية والإنجليزية، ومنها ترجمات «النبي» إلى لغات عدة، ودراسات عنه وعن أدب المهجر.
en: Kahlil Gibran (1883–1931) was born in Bsharri in Mount Lebanon and emigrated to Boston with his family at twelve. He first wrote in Arabic, including [The Broken Wings](/book/1966031?lang=en), an early Arabic novel, then in English, where [The Prophet](/book/98?lang=en) (1923) became one of the most translated books of the century.
With Mikhail Naimy and Elia Abu Madi he founded the Pen League in New York, which renewed Arabic writing in the diaspora.

ar: جرجي زيدان (1861–1914) أديب ومؤرخ وصحفي لبناني، وُلد في بيروت لأسرة فقيرة، ودرس الطب في الكلية السورية الإنجيلية ثم انتقل إلى مصر، حيث أسس عام 1892 مجلة «الهلال» التي ما زالت تصدر إلى اليوم.

اشتهر بسلسلة «روايات تاريخ الإسلام»، أكثر من عشرين رواية حكت التاريخ الإسلامي من الجاهلية إلى العصر المملوكي في قالب قصة حب ومغامرة، منها [فتاة غسان](/book/1966063) و[أرمانوسة المصرية](/book/1966269) و[عذراء قريش](/book/1966234) و[فتح الأندلس](/book/1966220) و[شجرة الدر](/book/1966265). وكتب إلى جانبها مؤلفات علمية مهمة مثل [تاريخ التمدن الإسلامي](/book/1966041) و[تاريخ آداب اللغة العربية](/book/1965870). جعلت رواياته التاريخ قريباً من القرّاء، فكانت لأجيال كثيرة المدخل الأول إلى تاريخهم.

وكان زيدان يكتب لقارئ عادي لا لعالم متخصص، فيشرح ويبسّط ويضع الحقائق التاريخية في الحواشي، ولذلك انتشرت رواياته انتشاراً واسعاً وطُبعت مرات كثيرة. وقد أخذ عليه بعض النقاد تساهله في بعض التفاصيل التاريخية، لكن فضله في تقريب التاريخ إلى عامة القرّاء لا يُنكر. وتجد معظم رواياته في المكتبة متاحة مجاناً على «صفحات»، فابدأ بأي عصر تحبه، فكل رواية قائمة بذاتها.
en: Jurji Zaydan (1861–1914), born in Beirut, studied medicine before moving to Cairo, where in 1892 he founded al-Hilal, a magazine still published today.

His twenty-odd historical novels retell Islamic history as romance and adventure, from [The Ghassanid Girl](/book/1966063?lang=en) to [The Conquest of al-Andalus](/book/1966220?lang=en); his scholarly [History of Islamic Civilization](/book/1966041?lang=en) is here too.

ar: مصطفى لطفي المنفلوطي (1876–1924) كاتب مصري من منفلوط في صعيد مصر، درس في الأزهر وتتلمذ على الإمام محمد عبده. اشتهر بمقالاته التي جمعها في [النظرات](/book/1965406) وبقصصه الحزينة في [العبرات](/book/1965853)، بأسلوب عاطفي بليغ جعله من أكثر الكتّاب قراءة في زمانه.

لم يكن المنفلوطي يعرف الفرنسية، فكان يستعين بمن يترجم له الروايات ثم يعيد صياغتها بعربيته الخاصة، فخرجت منها أعمال صارت جزءاً من الأدب العربي، مثل [ماجدولين](/book/1965648) عن رواية ألفونس كار، و[في سبيل التاج](/book/1965731) عن مسرحية فرانسوا كوبيه، و[الشاعر](/book/1965838) عن «سيرانو دي برجراك» لإدمون روستان، و[الفضيلة](/book/1965414) عن «بول وفرجيني».

ولم تخلُ كتابة المنفلوطي من نقد، فقد رأى فيها بعض النقاد عاطفية زائدة وميلاً إلى الحزن، لكنها علّمت أجيالاً من القرّاء العرب حب القراءة والبيان، وما زالت كتبه تُقرأ وتُطبع إلى اليوم. وتجد معظمها في المكتبة متاحاً مجاناً على «صفحات»، فابدأ بـ«العبرات» إن أحببت القصص، أو «النظرات» إن أحببت المقالات، وكلاهما يُقرأ في جلسات قليلة. فقد كان المنفلوطي معلماً للبيان قبل أن يكون كاتباً.
en: Mustafa Lutfi al-Manfaluti (1876–1924), from Manfalut in Upper Egypt, studied at al-Azhar under Muhammad Abduh and won a huge readership with the essays of [al-Nazarat](/book/1965406?lang=en) and the sad stories of [al-Abarat](/book/1965853?lang=en).

Knowing no French, he had novels translated for him and rewrote them in his own Arabic: [Magdoline](/book/1965648?lang=en) from Alphonse Karr, [For the Crown](/book/1965731?lang=en) from François Coppée, and [The Poet](/book/1965838?lang=en) from Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac.

ar: عبد الرحمن بن خلدون (732–808 هـ / 1332–1406 م) مؤرخ ومفكر وُلد في تونس لأسرة أندلسية الأصل، وتقلّب في المناصب بين بلاطات المغرب والأندلس، ثم اعتزل في قلعة ابن سلامة في الجزائر حيث كتب «المقدمة» في بضعة أشهر، وأمضى آخر سنواته قاضياً في القاهرة.

«المقدمة» هي الجزء الأول من كتابه الكبير في التاريخ «العِبَر»، لكنها صارت كتاباً قائماً بذاته، لأن ابن خلدون حاول فيها أن يفسّر قيام الدول وسقوطها بقوانين اجتماعية، فتحدث عن «العصبية» ودورة الدولة من البداوة إلى الحضارة إلى الهرم، ولهذا يعدّه كثيرون مؤسس علم الاجتماع. وفي المكتبة نصوص من مؤلفاته ودراسات عنها، منها [دراسات عن مقدمة ابن خلدون](/book/1964222) لساطع الحصري.

عاش ابن خلدون حياة مليئة بالتقلبات، فقد سُجن وتنقّل بين الدول وشهد الحروب، ويُروى أنه التقى القائد المغولي تيمورلنك خارج دمشق سنة 803 هـ (1401 م) وكتب عن لقائه به. ويرى كثير من الدارسين أن تجربته العملية في السياسة هي التي ألهمته نظرياته في «المقدمة». وتجد في المكتبة دراسات كثيرة عنه.
en: Ibn Khaldun (1332–1406) was born in Tunis to a family from al-Andalus, served the courts of North Africa and Granada, and wrote his Muqaddimah in a few months of retreat at the fortress of Qal'at Ibn Salama in Algeria; he died a judge in Cairo.
The Muqaddimah, the introduction to his universal history, explains the rise and fall of states through group solidarity ('asabiyya'), which is why he is often called a founder of sociology.

ar: أبو عثمان عمرو بن بحر الجاحظ (نحو 159–255 هـ / 776–868 م) إمام النثر العربي، وُلد في البصرة وعاش نحو تسعين عاماً، ولُقّب بالجاحظ لجحوظ عينيه. قرأ كل ما وقع في يده، حتى قيل إنه كان يستأجر دكاكين الورّاقين ليلاً ليقرأ ما فيها.

كتب في كل شيء تقريباً، بأسلوب يجمع العلم والفكاهة والاستطراد: «الحيوان» الذي جمع فيه معارف عصره عن الحيوان، و«البيان والتبيين» في البلاغة والخطابة، و«البخلاء» الذي رسم فيه صوراً ساخرة لبخلاء عصره ما زالت تُضحك القرّاء. وفي المكتبة طبعات قديمة من بعض مؤلفاته من مكتبة HathiTrust، وإن أردت أن تبدأ به فابدأ بـ«البخلاء» لتعرف لماذا ما زال الجاحظ حياً بعد أكثر من ألف عام.

ومات الجاحظ في البصرة وقد جاوز التسعين، وتقول الرواية المشهورة إن كتبه سقطت عليه وهو شيخ مريض فكانت سبب موته، وهي نهاية تليق برجل عاش بين الكتب. ويُعد كتابه «الحيوان» من أوائل الكتب العربية التي تأملت أثر البيئة في الكائنات. وما زالت كتبه تُقرأ وتُدرّس.
en: Al-Jahiz (c. 776–868) of Basra, the great master of Arabic prose, read everything he could find; it was said he rented booksellers' shops at night to read their stock.
His Book of Animals, his work on eloquence al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin and the satirical Book of Misers mix learning, wit and digression; the library holds old printed editions of several of his works.

ar: وليم شكسبير (1564–1616) أعظم كتّاب الإنجليزية وأكثر كتّاب المسرح تمثيلاً في العالم. وُلد في ستراتفورد أبون آفون، وعمل في لندن ممثلاً وكاتباً وشريكاً في فرقة مسرحية، وكتب نحو سبع وثلاثين مسرحية و154 سوناتة وقصائد طويلة.

تنقسم مسرحياته إلى مآسٍ مثل [هاملت](/book/1) و[ماكبث](/book/2) و[عطيل](/book/4) و[الملك لير](/book/5)، وكوميديات مثل [حلم ليلة صيف](/book/6) و[تاجر البندقية](/book/8)، ومسرحيات تاريخية عن ملوك إنجلترا. عرفها القارئ العربي مبكراً بترجمات خليل مطران وغيره، وما زالت عباراتها حيّة في لغات كثيرة. في المكتبة نصوصه الأصلية كاملة، ومعها مئات الطبعات والدراسات من مكتبة HathiTrust.

وما زال شكسبير يُترجم ويُمثَّل في العالم العربي، من المسارح الكبرى إلى عروض المدارس، ويقارن الدارسون كثيراً بين مسرحيته «أنطونيو وكليوباترا» و«مصرع كليوباترا» لأحمد شوقي. وإن كانت لغته صعبة عليك، فابدأ بقراءة ملخص المسرحية، ثم اقرأ نصها مع ترجمة عربية. وتجد في المكتبة كذلك [السوناتات](/book/11) كاملة. ومن عباراته التي صارت أمثالاً في الإنجليزية: «أكون أو لا أكون»، و«الدنيا كلها مسرح»، وكثير غيرها مما يستخدمه الناس دون أن يعرفوا مصدره.
en: William Shakespeare (1564–1616), born in Stratford-upon-Avon, actor, playwright and shareholder of a London company, wrote about thirty-seven plays and 154 sonnets.

The tragedies [Hamlet](/book/1?lang=en), [Macbeth](/book/2?lang=en), [Othello](/book/4?lang=en) and [King Lear](/book/5?lang=en), and comedies such as [A Midsummer Night's Dream](/book/6?lang=en), are here in full, with hundreds of editions and studies from HathiTrust.

ar: فيودور دوستويفسكي (1821–1881) روائي روسي يُعد من أعمق من كتبوا عن النفس الإنسانية. اعتُقل شاباً بسبب نشاطه في حلقة فكرية، وحُكم عليه بالإعدام ثم خُفف الحكم في اللحظة الأخيرة إلى أشغال شاقة في سيبيريا، وكتب عن تلك السنوات [ذكريات من بيت الموتى](/book/20).

رواياته الكبرى أسئلة كبرى في ثوب قصص: [الجريمة والعقاب](/book/12) عن طالب يقتل ثم يحاكمه ضميره، و[الأبله](/book/14) عن رجل طيب في عالم قاس، و[الإخوة كارامازوف](/book/13) عن الإيمان والحرية والأبوة. وكتب أيضاً أعمالاً أقصر جميلة مثل [الليالي البيضاء](/book/17) و[الفقراء](/book/19) و[المقامر](/book/18)، وهي مدخل لطيف إليه قبل الروايات الطويلة.

أثّر دوستويفسكي في الأدب والفلسفة من بعده تأثيراً هائلاً، فرأى فيه كثيرون رائداً لأدب القلق والأسئلة الوجودية، وقرأه العرب بشغف منذ نقل سامي الدروبي أعماله الكاملة إلى العربية. والمتاح هنا ترجماته الإنجليزية القديمة التي صارت في الملك العام. وأيسر رواياته للبداية «الليالي البيضاء»، وهي قصة حب قصيرة تُقرأ في جلسة واحدة. وفي المكتبة كذلك دراسات وكتب عنه بالعربية والإنجليزية، تساعدك على فهم عالمه.
en: Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821–1881) was sentenced to death in 1849 for his part in a radical circle, reprieved at the last moment and sent to hard labour in Siberia, which he described in [The House of the Dead](/book/20?lang=en).

His great novels, [Crime and Punishment](/book/12?lang=en), [The Idiot](/book/14?lang=en) and [The Brothers Karamazov](/book/13?lang=en), turn questions of guilt, faith and freedom into stories; [White Nights](/book/17?lang=en) is a gentle place to start.

ar: ليو تولستوي (1828–1910) روائي ومفكر روسي، وُلد في ضيعة ياسنايا بوليانا لأسرة من النبلاء، وشارك في حرب القرم جندياً، ثم كتب روايتين تُعدّان من قمم الرواية في العالم: [الحرب والسلم](/book/21) التي ترسم المجتمع الروسي في زمن حروب نابليون، و[آنا كارينينا](/book/22) التي تبدأ بجملتها الشهيرة عن الأسر السعيدة والتعيسة.

في سنواته الأخيرة تحوّل تولستوي إلى مفكر أخلاقي يدعو إلى البساطة واللاعنف، وكتب [مملكة الله في داخلكم](/book/28) الذي تأثر به غاندي، ورواية [البعث](/book/24). وكتب أيضاً قصصاً قصيرة وحكايات شعبية للناس البسطاء ما زالت تُقرأ للصغار والكبار. في المكتبة أعماله الكبرى بترجماتها الإنجليزية.

وغادر تولستوي بيته وهو في الثانية والثمانين بحثاً عن حياة بسيطة، فمرض في الطريق ومات في محطة قطار صغيرة عام 1910. وما زالت رواياته تُقرأ وتُقتبس في السينما والمسرح، ويرى كثير من النقاد أن «الحرب والسلم» أعظم رواية كُتبت. وإن كانت رواياته الكبرى طويلة عليك، فابدأ بأعماله القصيرة مثل «موت إيفان إيليتش». وتضم المكتبة مئات الكتب له وعنه بلغات مختلفة.
en: Leo Tolstoy (1828–1910), born at Yasnaya Polyana and a veteran of the Crimean War, wrote two of the summits of the novel, [War and Peace](/book/21?lang=en) and [Anna Karenina](/book/22?lang=en).
In later life he preached simplicity and non-violence in [The Kingdom of God Is Within You](/book/28?lang=en), a book that deeply influenced Gandhi.

ar: فيكتور هوغو (1802–1885) شاعر وروائي ومسرحي فرنسي، وأحد أعلام الحركة الرومانسية. كتب الشعر شاباً، ثم الرواية التاريخية «أحدب نوتردام» (1831) التي أحيت الاهتمام بالكاتدرائية الشهيرة، وانخرط في السياسة فعارض نابليون الثالث وعاش منفياً قرابة عشرين عاماً في جزر القنال.

في المنفى أتمّ روايته الكبرى [البؤساء](/book/44) (1862) عن جان فالجان، المحكوم السابق الذي يبحث عن الخلاص في مجتمع لا يغفر، وكتب [عمال البحر](/book/46) عن الصياد جيلييت وصراعه مع البحر. عرّب حافظ إبراهيم «البؤساء» في مطلع القرن العشرين، فصارت من أحب الروايات إلى القرّاء العرب. وحين مات هوغو خرجت حشود هائلة في جنازته في باريس.

وكتب هوغو للمسرح أيضاً، فكانت مسرحيته «هرناني» عام 1830 معركة أدبية بين الكلاسيكيين والرومانسيين انتهت بانتصار الرومانسية. ويُعد ديوانه «التأملات» من أجمل الشعر الفرنسي، وكتب كثيراً منه حزناً على ابنته ليوبولدين التي غرقت شابة. ودُفن في «البانتيون» في باريس، مقبرة عظماء فرنسا. وتجد في المكتبة أعماله الكبرى بترجماتها الإنجليزية، إلى جانب دراسات عنه وعن الحركة الرومانسية الفرنسية في القرن التاسع عشر.
en: Victor Hugo (1802–1885), leading voice of French Romanticism, wrote The Hunchback of Notre-Dame and spent nearly twenty years in exile in the Channel Islands for opposing Napoleon III.

There he finished [Les Misérables](/book/44?lang=en), the story of the convict Jean Valjean, and [Toilers of the Sea](/book/46?lang=en); the poet Hafez Ibrahim's Arabic version of Les Misérables made it a favourite of Arab readers.

ar: تشارلز ديكنز (1812–1870) أشهر روائيي العصر الفيكتوري في إنجلترا. عمل طفلاً في مصنع لتلميع الأحذية حين سُجن أبوه بسبب الديون، فبقيت صورة الفقر والطفولة المظلومة في قلب رواياته، من [أوليفر تويست](/book/31) إلى [ديفيد كوبرفيلد](/book/32) التي استلهم فيها كثيراً من حياته.

نشر ديكنز معظم رواياته فصولاً متتابعة، فكان القرّاء ينتظرون كل فصل جديد بشغف. ومن أشهر أعماله [قصة مدينتين](/book/30) عن الثورة الفرنسية، و[آمال كبيرة](/book/29)، و[ترنيمة عيد الميلاد](/book/33) عن البخيل سكروج الذي تزوره الأشباح فيتغير. تجمع رواياته بين الفكاهة والنقد الاجتماعي، وقد أسهمت في إصلاح أوضاع الفقراء والأطفال في بلاده.

وكان ديكنز قارئاً بارعاً لأعماله، فقرأ رواياته على الجمهور في جولات طويلة في بريطانيا وأمريكا لقيت نجاحاً هائلاً. وما زالت شخصياته مثل «أوليفر» و«سكروج» تعيش في السينما والمسرح، وصار اسمه نفسه صفة في الإنجليزية تصف الفقر القاسي في المدن الكبرى. وابدأ إن شئت بـ«ترنيمة عيد الميلاد»، فهي قصيرة ومحبوبة، ثم انتقل إلى «أوليفر تويست». وتضم المكتبة رواياته كلها تقريباً بلغتها الإنجليزية الأصلية.
en: Charles Dickens (1812–1870) worked in a boot-blacking factory as a boy while his father was in a debtors' prison, and poverty and wronged childhood run through his novels, from [Oliver Twist](/book/31?lang=en) to the largely autobiographical [David Copperfield](/book/32?lang=en).
Published in instalments, books such as [A Tale of Two Cities](/book/30?lang=en), [Great Expectations](/book/29?lang=en) and [A Christmas Carol](/book/33?lang=en) mixed comedy and social protest.

Jane Austen (1775–1817) grew up in a crowded rectory in the Hampshire village of Steventon, the seventh of eight children, writing comic sketches to amuse her family. She never married, lived quietly in Bath and then in a cottage at Chawton, and published her novels anonymously, signed only 'By a Lady'. She died in Winchester at forty-one.

Her six novels, from [Pride and Prejudice](/book/38?lang=en) to [Emma](/book/39?lang=en) and [Persuasion](/book/41?lang=en), turn the small world of country families, marriages and money into sharp, funny studies of character. Her ironic narration, slipping in and out of her heroines' thoughts, changed the way novels are written.

Samuel Clemens (1835–1910) grew up in Hannibal, Missouri, on the banks of the Mississippi, and worked as a printer's apprentice, a steamboat pilot, a silver prospector in Nevada and a newspaper reporter before he became Mark Twain. A comic story about a jumping frog made his name in 1865, and his lectures and travel books made him the most famous American writer of his time.

He drew on his boyhood for [The Adventures of Tom Sawyer](/book/48?lang=en) and [Adventures of Huckleberry Finn](/book/49?lang=en), and on his piloting years for [Life on the Mississippi](/book/53?lang=en). Late in life he lost his fortune in bad investments and paid his debts with a lecture tour around the world. He was born in a year of Halley's Comet and died when it returned.

Arthur Conan Doyle (1859–1930) was born in Edinburgh, trained as a doctor and wrote stories while waiting for patients at his practice in Southsea. Sherlock Holmes, modelled partly on his old teacher Joseph Bell, who could diagnose a patient's life at a glance, first appeared in 1887 and soon made Doyle one of the best-paid writers in the world.

He grew tired of his detective, killed him off in 1893 and was forced by his readers to bring him back. Doyle also wrote historical novels, the adventure [The Lost World](/book/61?lang=en) and campaigns for wrongly convicted men. Start with [The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes](/book/54?lang=en) and [The Hound of the Baskervilles](/book/55?lang=en).

Oscar Wilde (1854–1900) was born in Dublin, studied classics at Trinity College and Oxford, and became the most quotable man in London, the leading voice of the movement that preached art for art's sake. Between 1892 and 1895 his comedies filled the theatres, and his only novel, [The Picture of Dorian Gray](/book/62?lang=en), caused a sensation.

At the height of his fame he was convicted for his relationship with Lord Alfred Douglas and sentenced to two years of hard labour, an experience he wrote about in [De Profundis](/book/68?lang=en). He died in exile in Paris, poor and broken, at forty-six. [The Importance of Being Earnest](/book/63?lang=en) remains one of the funniest plays in English.

Franz Kafka (1883–1924) was born in Prague into a German-speaking Jewish family, studied law and spent his working life as a conscientious official at an insurance institute for workers' accidents. He wrote at night, in a few intense bursts, and published only a handful of stories in his lifetime.

Dying of tuberculosis at forty, he asked his friend Max Brod to burn all his manuscripts; Brod refused and published [The Trial](/book/70?lang=en), The Castle and much more. Kafka's dreamlike stories of guilt, bureaucracy and isolation gave the world the word 'Kafkaesque', and few twentieth-century writers have been more influential.

Plato (c. 428–348 BC) was born into an aristocratic family in Athens and became the devoted student of Socrates. After his teacher's trial and execution in 399 BC, he travelled, returned to Athens and founded the Academy, a school that lasted for centuries and counted Aristotle among its students.

Almost all his writings are dialogues in which Socrates questions his fellow citizens about justice, love, knowledge and the soul, from the [Apology](/book/75?lang=en) to the [Symposium](/book/76?lang=en) and the [Republic](/book/74?lang=en). Known to Arab philosophers as Aflatun, he was read closely by al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd, and Western philosophy has been called a series of footnotes to him.

Aristotle (384–322 BC), the son of a doctor from Stagira in northern Greece, studied at Plato's Academy for twenty years, tutored the young Alexander the Great and then founded his own school in Athens, the Lyceum, where he is said to have taught while walking.

He wrote on almost everything: logic, physics, biology, ethics, [politics](/book/84?lang=en), rhetoric and poetry, and his works became the foundation of learning for two thousand years. In the Arabic tradition he was called the First Teacher, and the great commentaries of [Ibn Rushd](/author/ibnrushd?lang=en) carried his thought back to medieval Europe.

Friedrich Nietzsche (1844–1900), the son of a Lutheran pastor, was appointed professor of classical philology at Basel at only twenty-four. His friendship with the composer Richard Wagner shaped his first book, [The Birth of Tragedy](/book/93?lang=en), and its bitter end shaped much of what followed. Ill health forced him to resign in 1879, and he spent ten restless years in Swiss and Italian lodgings, writing book after book.

In [Thus Spake Zarathustra](/book/91?lang=en), [Beyond Good and Evil](/book/92?lang=en) and his later works he questioned morality, religion and truth itself. He collapsed in Turin in 1889 and never recovered; his sister later bent his work toward nationalist causes he had despised. Few philosophers have been so influential, or so often misread.

Abu Ali ibn Sina (980–1037), known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara and had mastered the Quran, mathematics and medicine by his teens. After curing the Samanid ruler, he was allowed into the royal library, and he later said he had read Aristotle's Metaphysics forty times without understanding it until a small commentary by [al-Farabi](/author/farabi?lang=en) opened it for him.

He spent his life moving between courts in Persia, often as physician and vizier, writing at night and on the road. His Canon of Medicine was taught in European universities until the seventeenth century, and his Book of Healing is one of the great works of philosophy. The library holds several of his shorter treatises, on the soul, love and logic.

Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1058–1111), born in Tus in Khorasan, became the most celebrated scholar of his age as a professor at the Nizamiyya college in Baghdad. Then, in 1095, a spiritual crisis left him unable to speak in class. He gave up his post, lived for years as a wandering Sufi in Damascus and Jerusalem, and returned convinced that true knowledge comes from experience as well as reason.

His Incoherence of the Philosophers challenged the followers of Aristotle and provoked a famous reply from [Ibn Rushd](/author/ibnrushd?lang=en); his Revival of the Religious Sciences became one of the most read books in Islam; and his autobiography, The Deliverance from Error, is still studied, and was quoted by William James in [The Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en).

Jalal al-Din Rumi (1207–1273) was born in the region of Balkh, in today's Afghanistan and Tajikistan, and as a boy fled the Mongol invasions with his family, who settled in Konya in Anatolia. He became a respected teacher of religious law, until in 1244 he met a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, and the friendship transformed him into a poet.

His Persian lyric poems and his long Masnavi, a sea of stories and teachings sometimes called the Quran in Persian, are among the most loved works of Sufi literature, and his followers founded the Mevlevi order of whirling dervishes. Today he is one of the most widely read poets in the world, in Arabic, English and many other languages.

Omar Khayyam (1048–1131) of Nishapur was famous in his own time as a mathematician and astronomer: he wrote a major treatise on algebra that solved cubic equations geometrically, and helped reform the Persian calendar into one of the most accurate ever made. The short four-line poems attributed to him were written, it seems, for himself and his friends.

Many of the quatrains credited to him may be by other poets, but their mix of doubt, wine and wonder at the shortness of life won the world through Edward FitzGerald's [Rubaiyat](/book/120?lang=en) of 1859. In Arabic they are best known in Ahmed Rami's version, parts of which Umm Kulthum sang.

Jules Verne (1828–1905) grew up in the port city of Nantes, watching ships leave for distant lands. Sent to Paris to study law, he wrote for the theatre instead, until the publisher Pierre-Jules Hetzel accepted [Five Weeks in a Balloon](/book/126?lang=en) in 1863 and signed him for a series of 'extraordinary voyages' that lasted the rest of his life.

In more than sixty novels he took readers under the sea, to the Moon and around the world, mixing adventure with real science and geography. [Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea](/book/121?lang=en) and [Around the World in Eighty Days](/book/122?lang=en) made him one of the most translated authors in history and inspired generations of scientists and explorers.

Edgar Allan Poe (1809–1849) was born in Boston to travelling actors and orphaned before he was three. Raised by a Richmond merchant who later disowned him, he lived by his pen as a poet, critic and magazine editor, always short of money. His young wife Virginia died of tuberculosis in 1847, and two years later Poe was found delirious in Baltimore and died days later, in circumstances that are still a mystery.

He made the short story an art of total effect, wrote tales of terror such as [The Fall of the House of Usher](/book/128?lang=en), invented the detective story with 'The Murders in the Rue Morgue' and wrote 'The Raven', one of the most famous poems in English. French poets led by Baudelaire honoured him before America did.

Alexandre Dumas (1802–1870) was the grandson of a French nobleman and an enslaved woman of African descent in Saint-Domingue; his father became a general of the Revolution. Arriving in Paris as a clerk with little education, Dumas made his name in the theatre and then, with the collaborator Auguste Maquet, turned history into the most popular adventure novels of the century.

[The Three Musketeers](/book/133?lang=en) and [The Count of Monte Cristo](/book/132?lang=en) were followed by dozens more, earning fortunes that Dumas spent as fast as they came, on travel, newspapers and a fantastic château. In 2002 his remains were moved to the Panthéon in Paris among the great figures of France.

Mary Shelley (1797–1851) was the daughter of two radical writers, Mary Wollstonecraft, who died days after her birth, and the philosopher William Godwin. At sixteen she ran away with the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley, and at eighteen, during a rainy summer by Lake Geneva with Lord Byron, she began the story that became [Frankenstein](/book/137?lang=en).

Her life was marked by loss: three of her four children died young and Percy drowned in 1822. She supported herself by writing, edited her husband's poems and wrote [The Last Man](/book/138?lang=en), an early novel of a worldwide plague. Her mother's [Vindication of the Rights of Woman](/book/299?lang=en) is also in the library.

Bram Stoker (1847–1912) was born in Dublin, a sickly child confined to bed until he was seven, who grew into a university athlete. He worked as a civil servant and an unpaid theatre critic, until his admiration for the actor Henry Irving led him to London, where for twenty-seven years he managed Irving's Lyceum Theatre.

In his spare time he wrote novels and stories, and after years of research into folklore and Eastern Europe published [Dracula](/book/139?lang=en) in 1897. It was only moderately successful in his lifetime, but it gave the modern world its image of the vampire. His widow published [Dracula's Guest](/book/140?lang=en) after his death.

Herman Melville (1819–1891) was born in New York to a family ruined when he was a boy. At twenty he went to sea, sailed on a whaler to the Pacific, deserted in the Marquesas Islands and turned the adventure into [Typee](/book/143?lang=en), a bestseller that made him famous at twenty-seven.

His ambitions grew with each book, and [Moby-Dick](/book/141?lang=en), published in 1851, was misunderstood and sold poorly. He spent nineteen years as a customs inspector on the New York docks, writing poems and the stories [Bartleby, the Scrivener](/book/142?lang=en) and [Billy Budd](/book/144?lang=en), and died almost forgotten; he was rediscovered as a great writer in the 1920s.

Charles Darwin (1809–1882) left medical school in Edinburgh because he could not bear to watch operations, and studied at Cambridge to become a clergyman. Instead, at twenty-two, he joined the five-year voyage of HMS Beagle, described in [The Voyage of the Beagle](/book/147?lang=en), which gave him the observations of a lifetime.

Back in England he worked for twenty years at his country home in Kent before a letter from the naturalist Alfred Russel Wallace, who had reached the same idea, pushed him to publish [On the Origin of Species](/book/145?lang=en) in 1859. He went on to write [The Descent of Man](/book/146?lang=en) and books on barnacles, orchids and earthworms, and was buried in Westminster Abbey.

Isaac Newton (1643–1727) was born on a farm in Lincolnshire and studied at Cambridge. When the plague closed the university in 1665, he went home and, in about two years, laid the foundations of calculus, of his theory of light and colour and of the idea of universal gravitation.

His Principia of 1687 explained the movements of the planets and the tides with the same laws that govern a falling apple, and [Opticks](/book/150?lang=en) showed that white light is made of colours. Later in life he ran the Royal Mint, chasing counterfeiters, and presided over the Royal Society, while privately studying alchemy and theology.

Karl Marx (1818–1883) was born in Trier in western Germany, studied law and philosophy and became a radical journalist. Expelled from Germany, France and Belgium for his writings, he settled in London in 1849, where he lived in poverty with his family, supported by his friend and collaborator Friedrich Engels.

With Engels he wrote [The Communist Manifesto](/book/151?lang=en) in 1848; in the reading room of the British Museum he spent years on Capital, his analysis of how capitalism works. Whatever one thinks of the movements made in his name, few thinkers have had as great an influence on politics, history and economics.

Immanuel Kant (1724–1804) spent his whole life in and around Königsberg in East Prussia, where he taught at the university for decades and kept such regular habits that, according to legend, neighbours set their clocks by his afternoon walk. He was fifty-seven when he published the Critique of Pure Reason, which changed philosophy.

Answering [David Hume](/book/277?lang=en), who he said woke him from his dogmatic slumber, Kant asked what we can know, what we ought to do and what we may hope, and gave the world the categorical imperative and the motto of the Enlightenment, 'Dare to know'. His short essay [Perpetual Peace](/book/157?lang=en) is his most accessible work.

Sigmund Freud (1856–1939) grew up in Vienna in a Jewish family and trained as a neurologist. After studying hypnosis with the famous Charcot in Paris, he began listening to his patients talk freely about their dreams and memories, and developed from this practice a new theory of the mind and a new kind of treatment: psychoanalysis.

From his consulting room at Berggasse 19 he published [The Interpretation of Dreams](/book/159?lang=en) and a stream of books that changed psychology, literature and everyday language. In 1938, after the Nazis took over Austria, he fled to London, where he died the following year. [A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis](/book/162?lang=en) is the best place to begin.

Johann Wolfgang von Goethe (1749–1832) was born in Frankfurt and trained as a lawyer, but at twenty-four his novel [The Sorrows of Young Werther](/book/166?lang=en) made him famous across Europe. Invited to the small court of Weimar, he served as a minister for years while writing poems, plays and novels, and pursuing serious research in botany, anatomy and the theory of colour.

His friendship with the poet Schiller and his journey to Italy shaped German classicism, and his [Faust](/book/165?lang=en), the work of sixty years, is the summit of German literature. Goethe admired the Persian poet Hafez and the Quran, and his West-Eastern Divan was an early bridge between European and Islamic poetry.

Miguel de Cervantes (1547–1616) lived a life as adventurous as any novel. As a soldier he was wounded at the naval battle of Lepanto in 1571 and lost the use of his left hand; on his way home he was captured by Barbary corsairs and spent five years as a captive in Algiers, where he tried to escape four times before he was ransomed.

Back in Spain he worked as a tax collector, went to prison more than once and wrote plays and stories with little success, until [Don Quixote](/book/168?lang=en) in 1605 made him famous. He died in Madrid in April 1616, the same month as Shakespeare. Memories of Algiers, and a pretend Arab historian, appear throughout his work.

Dante Alighieri (1265–1321) was born in Florence and, as a boy of nine, saw Beatrice Portinari, the woman who would inspire his poetry for the rest of his life, as he tells in [La Vita Nuova](/book/171?lang=en). He became a poet, a soldier and a politician, and in 1302 was exiled by his political enemies under threat of death.

He never returned to Florence. In exile, moving between the courts of northern Italy, he wrote [The Divine Comedy](/book/170?lang=en), placing friends and enemies in Hell, Purgatory and Paradise. He died in Ravenna, where he is buried, and the city of Florence still keeps an empty tomb for him.

Homer is the name the Greeks gave to the poet of the [Iliad](/book/172?lang=en) and the [Odyssey](/book/173?lang=en), probably composed in Ionia in the eighth century BC. Ancient tradition pictured him as a blind singer, and modern scholars have shown that the poems grew out of a long tradition of oral poetry, sung by bards who used repeated phrases to compose as they performed.

Whether one poet or many, Homer stands at the beginning of European literature, and the Greeks learned their heroes, gods and values from him. Sulayman al-Bustani's verse translation of the Iliad, published in 1904 with a long introduction, was a milestone in Arabic letters.

Anton Chekhov (1860–1904) was the grandson of a serf who bought his family's freedom. He studied medicine in Moscow and paid for his studies and his family's keep by writing hundreds of humorous sketches for magazines. 'Medicine is my lawful wife and literature my mistress,' he once wrote, and he practised both all his life.

In 1890 he crossed Siberia to study the prison island of Sakhalin. His short stories, like [The Lady with the Dog](/book/178?lang=en), and his plays for the Moscow Art Theatre, like [Uncle Vanya](/book/175?lang=en), transformed both forms with their quiet, open endings. He died of tuberculosis in Germany at forty-four.

H. G. Wells (1866–1946) was the son of a failing shopkeeper and a lady's maid, and worked as a draper's apprentice before winning a scholarship to study science under T. H. Huxley, Darwin's great defender. Between 1895 and 1901 he wrote the scientific romances that founded modern science fiction, [The Time Machine](/book/179?lang=en), [The War of the Worlds](/book/180?lang=en) and The Invisible Man among them.

He went on to write social novels, popular history such as [A Short History of the World](/book/184?lang=en) and books urging world government, met Lenin and Roosevelt, and imagined tanks, air war and the atomic bomb before they existed. Few writers have thought so hard about the future.

Robert Louis Stevenson (1850–1894) came from a family of Edinburgh lighthouse engineers and was expected to follow them, but chose writing, despite lungs so weak he was often bedridden. He travelled constantly in search of health, married the American Fanny Osbourne and wrote [Treasure Island](/book/185?lang=en) for her son.

[Kidnapped](/book/187?lang=en), Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde and [A Child's Garden of Verses](/book/188?lang=en) followed, and in 1890 he settled in Samoa, where the islanders called him Tusitala, the teller of tales. He died there at forty-four and is buried on a hilltop above his home.

Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson (1832–1898), a shy mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford, who was also a deacon, a pioneering photographer and the author of books on logic. On a boat trip in July 1862 he made up a story for the three daughters of the college dean, and ten-year-old Alice Liddell asked him to write it down.

The result, [Alice's Adventures in Wonderland](/book/189?lang=en), followed by [Through the Looking-Glass](/book/190?lang=en) and [The Hunting of the Snark](/book/191?lang=en), changed children's books forever with nonsense, wordplay and logic games that delight adults as much as children.

Hans Christian Andersen (1805–1875) was the son of a poor shoemaker and a washerwoman in Odense, Denmark. At fourteen he went alone to Copenhagen to become a singer or an actor, failed at both, and was saved by patrons who sent him to school. He wrote novels, plays and travel books, but his fame came from the tales he began publishing in 1835.

Stories like The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling, many drawn from his own sense of being an outsider, have been translated into more languages than almost any other books. His [Fairy Tales](/book/192?lang=en) are in the library. He once stayed so long as a guest in Charles Dickens's house that Dickens pinned a note to the mirror after he left.

Abu al-Walid ibn Rushd (1126–1198), known in Europe as Averroes, came from a family of judges in Córdoba and served as chief judge of Seville and Córdoba and as physician to the Almohad caliphs. When the philosopher [Ibn Tufail](/author/ibntufail?lang=en) introduced him to the caliph, he was asked to explain the works of Aristotle, a task that became his life's work.

His commentaries made him 'the Commentator' for medieval European scholars, and his Decisive Treatise argued that philosophy and religion do not contradict each other. His Incoherence of the Incoherence answered [al-Ghazali](/author/ghazali?lang=en). Late in life he fell from favour and his books were burned, before he was pardoned shortly before his death in Marrakesh.

Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham (c. 965–c. 1040), known in Europe as Alhazen, was born in Basra and went to Cairo to serve the Fatimid caliph al-Hakim, who wanted to control the floods of the Nile. According to a famous story, when he realised the project was impossible, he pretended to be mad to escape the caliph's anger, and used his years of confinement to study.

His Book of Optics showed through careful experiments that we see because light enters the eye, and described the camera obscura. Translated into Latin, it influenced European science for centuries, down to Kepler and [Newton](/book/150?lang=en), and his insistence on testing ideas by experiment makes him one of the founders of scientific method.

Ahmed Shawqi (1868–1932) was born in Cairo and raised near the court of the Khedive, who sent him to study law in France. He became the court poet of Egypt, and when the British exiled him to Spain during the First World War, the years in Andalusia inspired some of his most beautiful poems of longing for home.

In 1927 poets from across the Arab world crowned him the Prince of Poets. His collected poems, al-Shawqiyyat, revived classical Arabic verse, and he brought verse drama into Arabic with plays such as [The Death of Cleopatra](/book/1966170?lang=en) and Majnun Layla. Many of his poems live on in the voices of Umm Kulthum and Mohammed Abdel Wahab.

Qasim Amin (1863–1908) was an Egyptian judge who studied law in France and returned convinced that his country's progress depended on the education and freedom of women. His book [The Liberation of Women](/book/1966246?lang=en) (1899) argued for girls' education and against the seclusion of women, and caused one of the great debates of modern Arab thought.

He answered his critics the following year with The New Woman, and he was among the founders of the Egyptian University, the forerunner of Cairo University. He died at forty-five, but his books are still discussed wherever women's rights are debated in the Arab world.

Muhammad Abduh (1849–1905) was born in a village of the Nile Delta, studied at al-Azhar and became a disciple of the reformer Jamal al-Din al-Afghani. Exiled after the Urabi revolt of 1882, he published with al-Afghani in Paris the journal al-Urwa al-Wuthqa, which was read across the Muslim world.

Allowed to return to Egypt, he worked to reform al-Azhar and the religious courts and became Grand Mufti in 1899. His Treatise on the Unity of God and his lessons in Quranic commentary argued that Islam welcomes reason and modern science. Among those he influenced were [Qasim Amin](/author/amin?lang=en) and [al-Manfaluti](/author/manfaluti?lang=en).

Abu Nasr al-Farabi (c. 872–950) came from Central Asia, studied in Baghdad and spent his last years at the court of Sayf al-Dawla in Aleppo before dying in Damascus. He was called the Second Teacher, after Aristotle himself, because he did so much to organise and explain Greek logic and philosophy in Arabic.

His most famous book, The Opinions of the People of the Virtuous City, imagines an ideal state ruled by a philosopher, in the spirit of Plato's [Republic](/book/74?lang=en). He also wrote one of the most important books on music theory in Arabic. [Ibn Sina](/author/avicenna?lang=en) said that only al-Farabi's commentary helped him understand Aristotle's Metaphysics.

Abu Bakr ibn Tufail (c. 1105–1185) was born near Granada and became physician and adviser to the Almohad caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf in Marrakesh. He was a patron as well as a philosopher: it was he who introduced the young [Ibn Rushd](/author/ibnrushd?lang=en) to the caliph and encouraged him to explain Aristotle.

His only surviving book, [Hayy ibn Yaqzan](/book/1966195?lang=en), tells of a child raised by a gazelle on a desert island who discovers the truth about nature and God by reason alone. Translated into Latin in 1671 and English in 1708, it was read widely in Europe, and some see in it an ancestor of [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en).

Ibn Hazm (994–1064) was born in Córdoba, the son of a vizier, and grew up in the palace world of the Umayyad caliphate just as it was collapsing into civil war. He took part in politics, was imprisoned and exiled more than once, and finally devoted himself to scholarship, writing on law, theology, history and comparative religion.

He is best loved today for The Ring of the Dove, a book about love written in his youth in Játiva, full of stories and verses about falling in love, separation, loyalty and loss, many from his own life. It is one of the most personal and tender books of Andalusian literature.

Abu al-Hasan al-Mas'udi (c. 896–956) was born in Baghdad and spent much of his life travelling: through Persia, India, the coasts of East Africa and the lands around the Caspian Sea, before settling in Egypt, where he died. He was curious about everything, peoples, religions, kings, geography and wonders.

His most famous work, The Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems, is a world history that begins with creation and runs through the histories of many nations to the caliphs of his own day, written with a storyteller's gift. European scholars have called him the Herodotus of the Arabs; see [Herodotus](/author/homerus?lang=en).

Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari (839–923) was born in Amol in Tabaristan, near the Caspian Sea, and travelled for years in search of knowledge before settling in Baghdad, where he taught and wrote until his death. He was so productive that later writers said he wrote forty pages a day for forty years.

His History of the Prophets and Kings is the most important early Arabic history, recording reports with their chains of transmitters so that readers could judge them, and his commentary on the Quran became a standard work. Later historians, among them [Ibn Khaldun](/author/khaldun?lang=en), built on his work.

Abu al-Hasan al-Mawardi (974–1058) was born in Basra, became a judge and a leading scholar of the Shafi'i school of law, and served the Abbasid caliphs in Baghdad as an envoy and adviser at a time when real power was held by others.

His Ordinances of Government is one of the first systematic works of Islamic political theory, describing the duties of the caliph, ministers, judges and governors. His Ethics of Religion and of This World, a book of practical wisdom on learning, friendship and conduct, is still read today.

Muhyi al-Din ibn Arabi (1165–1240), known as the Greatest Master, was born in Murcia in al-Andalus. As a young man he met the philosopher [Ibn Rushd](/author/ibnrushd?lang=en) in Córdoba, and then followed the Sufi path across North Africa and the East, to Mecca, where he began his vast Meccan Revelations, and finally to Damascus, where he died.

His books, above all The Bezels of Wisdom, made him the most influential and most debated mystical thinker in Islam. His love poems, The Interpreter of Desires, include the famous lines in which the poet's heart becomes able to take every form. Compare the poetry of [Rumi](/author/rumi?lang=en), his younger contemporary.

Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi (936–1013), known in Europe as Albucasis, was born in Madinat al-Zahra near Córdoba and served as physician at the Umayyad court. He spent his life practising medicine and teaching, and is considered the greatest surgeon of the medieval Islamic world.

His medical encyclopedia, al-Tasrif, ends with a book on surgery that describes operations step by step and illustrates some two hundred instruments, many of his own design. Translated into Latin in the twelfth century, it was used in European medical schools for five hundred years.

Badi al-Zaman al-Jazari (1136–1206) was an engineer who served the Artuqid rulers of Diyarbakir, in the upper Mesopotamian region known as al-Jazira, for twenty-five years. At the request of his prince he wrote down everything he had built in his Book of Knowledge of Ingenious Mechanical Devices, completed in 1206.

The book describes some fifty machines with precise drawings, among them water clocks such as the famous elephant clock, musical automata, fountains and water-raising pumps, and uses mechanisms that anticipate later engineering. It shows a craftsman's joy in machines that are both useful and beautiful. Note that the library also lists, under his name, works by a later scholar of Quranic readings also called al-Jazari.

Abu Abdallah al-Idrisi (1100–1165) was born in Ceuta, studied in Córdoba and travelled widely before the Norman king Roger II of Sicily invited him to Palermo to make a description of the whole known world. With the help of travellers and merchants, he worked on it for some fifteen years.

The result, completed in 1154, was The Book of Pleasant Journeys into Faraway Lands, with a world map in seventy sections and a great map engraved on silver. It was one of the most accurate geographies of the Middle Ages and is a monument to cooperation between Arab and European scholars.

Ibn Jubayr (1145–1217), born in Valencia, was secretary to the governor of Granada when, according to a well-known story, he was forced to drink wine and, in remorse, set out on the pilgrimage to Mecca. His journey, from 1183 to 1185, took him through Egypt under Saladin, the Hejaz, Iraq, Syria and Norman Sicily.

His Rihla, the travel diary he kept along the way, is one of the most vivid travel books in Arabic, full of the cities, sea storms, pilgrims and rulers he saw. He made two more journeys east and died in Alexandria. Compare it with [The Travels of Marco Polo](/book/254?lang=en), written a century later.

Abu Muhammad al-Qasim al-Hariri (1054–1122) was a wealthy official of Basra and a master of the Arabic language. His fifty Maqamat follow the wanderings of the eloquent rogue Abu Zayd of Saruj, who in every episode tricks his audience with a dazzling speech, as told by the narrator al-Harith ibn Hammam.

The Maqamat are a festival of wordplay, rhymed prose and rare vocabulary, and for centuries they were memorised and studied across the Arab world; illustrated manuscripts such as the famous one painted by al-Wasiti in 1237 are treasures of Islamic art. He followed the model created by [al-Hamadhani](/author/hamadhani?lang=en).

Badi al-Zaman al-Hamadhani (969–1007), the Wonder of the Age, was born in Hamadan and became famous for his memory and his gift for improvisation, winning a celebrated contest of eloquence against the older scholar al-Khwarizmi. He died in Herat at about forty.

He invented the maqama, a short story in rhymed prose in which the narrator Isa ibn Hisham keeps meeting the brilliant trickster Abu al-Fath al-Iskandari. The form was perfected by [al-Hariri](/author/hariri?lang=en), and centuries later al-Muwaylihi borrowed his narrator's name for [Hadith Isa ibn Hisham](/book/1966000?lang=en).

Abu Nuwas (c. 756–814) was born in Ahvaz to an Arab father and a Persian mother, grew up in Basra and went to Baghdad, where he became a companion of the caliph Harun al-Rashid and, above all, his son al-Amin. He was famous for his wit, his learning and his scandalous life.

He mocked the old custom of opening poems with weeping over abandoned campsites and made wine and pleasure his subjects instead, but he also wrote hunting poems and, late in life, poems of repentance. He became a legendary figure, appearing as a clever trickster in the Arabian Nights.

Imru al-Qais (c. 501–544), the son of a king of the tribe of Kinda, is said to have been banished by his father for writing love poetry. When he heard that his father had been murdered, he declared, 'Today wine, tomorrow business', and spent the rest of his life trying to avenge him and win back the kingdom.

According to legend, he travelled to Constantinople to seek the emperor's help and died on the way home. His Mu'allaqa, which begins 'Stop, let us weep at the memory of a beloved and a dwelling', is one of the most famous poems in Arabic, and he is often called the prince of the pre-Islamic poets.

Rifa'a al-Tahtawi (1801–1873), from Tahta in Upper Egypt, was a young scholar of al-Azhar when he was sent to Paris in 1826 as the religious guide of an Egyptian student mission. He spent five years there, learned French and recorded everything he saw in [Takhlis al-Ibriz](/book/1966273?lang=en), a classic of Arabic travel writing.

Back in Egypt he founded the School of Languages, translated or supervised the translation of many European books and edited the official gazette. He is one of the founders of the Arab renaissance of the nineteenth century, and his ideas on education, the nation and women's learning prepared the way for later reformers.

Herodotus (c. 484–425 BC) was born in Halicarnassus, today's Bodrum in Turkey, and travelled widely in Egypt, Babylon, the Black Sea and Greece, asking questions everywhere he went. His Histories tell the story of the wars between the Greeks and the Persian Empire, and of the peoples involved, their customs, their gods and their legends.

Cicero called him the Father of History, and he was the first to set out to investigate the causes of events rather than simply record them. His book on Egypt, which the library also holds on its own as An Account of Egypt, is full of wonders, some true and some not, and remains a delight to read.

Thucydides (c. 460–400 BC) was an Athenian general who survived the great plague of Athens and was exiled for twenty years after failing to save the city of Amphipolis. He used his exile to write the history of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta, interviewing participants on both sides.

His History, left unfinished, is famous for its rigour and its speeches, among them Pericles' Funeral Oration and the cold debate between Athens and the island of Melos. It is still read by students of politics and war as a study of power, fear and human nature.

Plutarch (c. 46–after 119) lived in the small town of Chaeronea in Greece and served as a priest at the oracle of Delphi. He was a philosopher, a teacher and a tireless writer who knew the Roman elite of his day while remaining devoted to his home town.

His Parallel Lives pair famous Greeks and Romans, Alexander and Caesar, Demosthenes and Cicero, to compare their characters, and his many essays on morals cover everything from anger to the education of children. Shakespeare took the plot of [Julius Caesar](/book/9?lang=en) from Plutarch, as did many writers after him.

Edward Gibbon (1737–1794) was a sickly child from a wealthy English family. At sixteen he converted to Catholicism at Oxford, and his father sent him to Lausanne, where he returned to Protestantism and educated himself in history and languages. In Rome in 1764, sitting among the ruins of the Capitol, he conceived the idea of writing about the city's decline.

The six volumes of his History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, published between 1776 and 1788, cover more than thirteen centuries, from the Antonine emperors to the fall of Constantinople, in a famously elegant and ironic style. His chapters on the rise of Islam were remarkably sympathetic for their time.

Marco Polo (1254–1324) was born in Venice into a family of merchants. At seventeen he set out with his father and uncle across Asia to the court of Kublai Khan, where he served the Mongol emperor for many years and travelled on his behalf through China and beyond.

Returning to Venice after twenty-four years away, he was captured in a war with Genoa, and in prison dictated his adventures to a fellow prisoner, producing [The Travels of Marco Polo](/book/254?lang=en). For centuries it was Europe's main source of knowledge about the East, and it inspired explorers, Columbus among them.

Marcus Aurelius (121–180) was adopted as heir by the emperor Antoninus Pius and ruled Rome from 161 until his death. He had been trained in Stoic philosophy since his youth, and he tried to live by it through a reign full of trouble: a devastating plague, floods and long wars on the Danube frontier.

He never wrote for the public. His private notes, the [Meditations](/book/255?lang=en), were kept by those around him and survived by chance, and today they are among the most widely read books of antiquity. His son Commodus, who succeeded him, could hardly have been more different.

Sun Tzu, Master Sun, is traditionally said to have been a general in the service of the king of Wu in the sixth century BC. According to a famous story, the king tested him by asking him to drill the palace women as soldiers, and when they laughed at his orders, Sun Tzu executed the king's two favourite concubines who commanded them, and the rest obeyed.

Historians are not sure he existed, and the book bearing his name may have been put together later, but [The Art of War](/book/256?lang=en) is the most famous work on strategy ever written. Its ideas on deception, preparation and winning without fighting are studied in business and politics as well as in war.

Lao Tzu, the Old Master, is said to have been a keeper of the archives at the Zhou court in the sixth century BC. According to legend, tired of the decline of the kingdom, he rode west on a water buffalo, and the guardian of the frontier pass asked him to write down his wisdom before he left. The result was the Tao Te Ching, in about five thousand characters.

Whether he was one man or a legend, the Tao Te Ching, with its teachings on simplicity, gentleness and non-action, became the founding text of Taoism and one of the most translated books in the world. Tradition says that Confucius once met him; read [The Analects](/book/258?lang=en) to compare their visions.

Kong Qiu, known as Confucius (551–479 BC), was born in the state of Lu, in today's Shandong, into a family of modest means. He held minor official posts, then spent some fourteen years travelling from state to state looking for a ruler who would put his ideas of good government into practice, without success.

He devoted himself to teaching, and tradition says he had three thousand students. His conversations, recorded by his disciples in [The Analects](/book/258?lang=en), put humaneness, learning, family duty and proper conduct at the centre of life, and shaped Chinese civilisation for more than two thousand years.

Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527) served the Florentine republic for fourteen years as a senior official and diplomat, meeting kings, popes and the ruthless Cesare Borgia. When the Medici family returned to power in 1512 he lost his post, was imprisoned and tortured, and retired to his small farm outside Florence.

There, in the evenings, he put on his best clothes to read the ancient historians, and wrote [The Prince](/book/259?lang=en), his Discourses on Livy and the comedy The Mandrake. His frank description of how power really works made his name a byword for cunning, but he was also a passionate defender of republics.

Adam Smith (1723–1790) was born in Kirkcaldy, Scotland, studied at Glasgow and Oxford and became professor of moral philosophy at Glasgow. His [Theory of Moral Sentiments](/book/263?lang=en) made his name in 1759, and a few years later he travelled in France as tutor to a young duke, meeting Voltaire and the French economists.

Back in Scotland he spent ten years on An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations (1776), which explained the division of labour, markets and free trade and founded modern economics. He ended his life, with some irony, as a commissioner of customs in Edinburgh.

John Stuart Mill (1806–1873) received one of the most intense educations ever recorded: his father taught him Greek at three and Latin at eight, and by his teens he was writing on economics. At twenty he fell into a deep depression and found his way out through the poetry of Wordsworth, an experience that taught him the value of feeling alongside reason.

He worked for thirty-five years at the East India Company, wrote on logic, economics and politics, and shared his intellectual life with Harriet Taylor, whom he married in 1851. As a Member of Parliament he proposed votes for women in 1867. His [On Liberty](/book/264?lang=en), [Utilitarianism](/book/265?lang=en) and [The Subjection of Women](/book/266?lang=en) are still at the centre of debate.

John Locke (1632–1704) trained as a physician at Oxford and became adviser to the Earl of Shaftesbury, a leading opponent of the king. Suspected of plotting, he fled to the Netherlands in 1683 and returned only after the Revolution of 1688, when he published the works that made him famous.

His Essay Concerning Human Understanding argued that the mind begins as a blank slate filled by experience, and his Two Treatises of Government defended natural rights to life, liberty and property and government by consent. His Letter Concerning Toleration argued for religious freedom. His ideas shaped the American Declaration of Independence and modern liberal thought.

Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679) liked to say that he was born prematurely when his mother heard that the Spanish Armada was coming, so that 'fear and I were born twins'. He spent much of his life as tutor and secretary to the aristocratic Cavendish family, met Galileo in Italy and was fascinated by geometry.

During the English Civil War he lived in exile in Paris, where he taught mathematics to the future King Charles II and wrote [Leviathan](/book/270?lang=en) (1651), arguing that only a powerful sovereign can save people from a war of all against all. He lived to ninety-one and was translating Homer in his eighties.

Jean-Jacques Rousseau (1712–1778) was born in Geneva, lost his mother days after his birth, ran away from an apprenticeship at fifteen and lived for years as a wanderer, a music copyist and the protégé of Madame de Warens. In 1750 an essay arguing that civilisation had corrupted humanity won a prize and made him famous overnight.

In 1762 he published both [The Social Contract](/book/271?lang=en) and [Emile](/book/273?lang=en); both were condemned, and he had to flee. His Confessions, one of the first modern autobiographies, admits among other things that he placed his own five children in a foundling hospital. Few writers have influenced politics, education and the romantic idea of the self so deeply.

René Descartes (1596–1650) was educated by the Jesuits, served as a gentleman soldier, and on a winter night in 1619, shut in a stove-heated room in Germany, had the series of dreams that convinced him to rebuild all knowledge from scratch. He spent most of his adult life in the Netherlands, where he could work in peace.

His [Discourse on the Method](/book/274?lang=en) and Meditations made 'I think, therefore I am' the starting point of modern philosophy, and his invention of coordinate geometry joined algebra and geometry for good. Invited to Stockholm by Queen Christina, who wanted lessons at five in the morning, he caught pneumonia and died there in the winter of 1650.

Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was born in Amsterdam to a family of Portuguese Jewish merchants. At twenty-three he was expelled from the Jewish community for his views, and he spent the rest of his life quietly, grinding lenses for telescopes and microscopes and corresponding with the scientists of Europe. He refused a professorship at Heidelberg so as to keep his freedom of thought.

His Theological-Political Treatise, published anonymously in 1670, argued for freedom of thought and a historical reading of scripture; it is also in the library in Arabic. His [Ethics](/book/276?lang=en) appeared after his death at forty-four, probably hastened by the glass dust of his work, and made him one of the great philosophers of freedom.

David Hume (1711–1776) was born in Edinburgh and wrote his [Treatise of Human Nature](/book/278?lang=en) in his twenties, in France. His scepticism about religion cost him professorships at Edinburgh and Glasgow, but his essays and his History of England made him famous and comfortable.

As secretary to the British embassy in Paris he was adored in the salons, and in Edinburgh he was the warm centre of the Scottish Enlightenment and a close friend of [Adam Smith](/author/smith?lang=en). His [Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding](/book/277?lang=en) woke Kant from his dogmatic slumber. He faced death with a calm and humour that astonished his visitors.

François-Marie Arouet (1694–1778), who called himself Voltaire, was imprisoned twice in the Bastille as a young man for his satirical verses. Exiled to England, he returned full of admiration for its freedoms and wrote the [Letters on England](/book/281?lang=en), which were burned in Paris.

He lived for years with the scientist Émilie du Châtelet, spent a stormy period at the court of Frederick the Great and finally settled at Ferney, near the Swiss border, from where he campaigned against religious intolerance and miscarriages of justice. He wrote plays, history and poetry, but his tales, [Candide](/book/279?lang=en) and [Zadig](/book/280?lang=en), are what most readers love today.

Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) was the son of a wealthy Danzig merchant and a successful novelist. His great work, The World as Will and Representation, appeared in 1818 and was almost entirely ignored; when he taught in Berlin, he scheduled his lectures at the same hour as Hegel's, and almost no students came.

He spent the rest of his life in Frankfurt with a succession of poodles, convinced of his own genius, until his collection of essays, Parerga and Paralipomena, finally brought him fame in 1851; a selection is in the library as [Essays](/book/284?lang=en). He was the first major Western philosopher to draw seriously on Indian thought, calling the Upanishads the consolation of his life.

Ralph Waldo Emerson (1803–1882) was a Boston minister who resigned his church in 1832 because he could no longer accept its rituals. After meeting Carlyle, Coleridge and Wordsworth in Europe, he settled in Concord, Massachusetts, and became America's best-known lecturer and the centre of the Transcendentalist movement.

His essay Nature and his address The American Scholar urged Americans to think for themselves, and his [Essays](/book/286?lang=en) gave the world 'Self-Reliance'. He encouraged the young Thoreau, praised the unknown Whitman, and loved the Persian poets Hafez and Saadi, some of whose verses he translated into English.

Henry David Thoreau (1817–1862) was born in Concord, Massachusetts, studied at Harvard and worked in his family's pencil business, as a surveyor and as a handyman in Emerson's house. From 1845 to 1847 he lived alone in a cabin by Walden Pond, the experience behind [Walden](/book/287?lang=en).

In 1846 he spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a tax that supported slavery and the war with Mexico, and his essay Civil Disobedience, born from that night, inspired Gandhi and Martin Luther King. He died of tuberculosis at forty-four, leaving journals that fill thousands of pages of observations of nature.

Walt Whitman (1819–1892) grew up on Long Island and in Brooklyn, left school at eleven and worked as a printer, teacher and newspaper editor. In 1855 he published the first [Leaves of Grass](/book/289?lang=en) himself, and spent the rest of his life revising and expanding it.

During the Civil War he went to Washington to look for his wounded brother and stayed for years, volunteering in the military hospitals, sitting with thousands of wounded soldiers. His elegies for Abraham Lincoln are among his most famous poems. The library also holds an Arabic selection of Leaves of Grass.

Emily Dickinson (1830–1886) spent almost all her life in her family's house in Amherst, Massachusetts. After a year at a women's seminary she withdrew more and more from society, dressing in white and receiving few visitors, though she kept up a lively correspondence with friends and with the critic Thomas Wentworth Higginson.

She wrote nearly eighteen hundred poems, sewing many into small handmade booklets, and published only a handful. Her sister discovered them after her death, and a complete edition faithful to her dashes and capital letters appeared only in 1955. Her [Poems](/book/290?lang=en) made her one of the greatest poets in English.

William Wordsworth (1770–1850) was born in Cockermouth in the Lake District and orphaned young. As a student he went to France during the Revolution and was swept up in its hopes, and he left behind a French daughter. Back in England he formed a close friendship with Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and together they published [Lyrical Ballads](/book/291?lang=en) in 1798.

He settled with his sister Dorothy at Dove Cottage in Grasmere and spent his life writing about nature, memory and the growth of the mind, above all in his long autobiographical poem, The Prelude, published after his death. He became Poet Laureate in 1843.

John Keats (1795–1821) was the son of a London stable keeper, lost both parents young, and trained as a surgeon at Guy's Hospital before giving up medicine for poetry. His first books were savagely reviewed, but in a few months of 1819, while nursing his grief for his brother Tom and in love with Fanny Brawne, he wrote the great odes.

Already ill with tuberculosis, he went to Rome hoping the climate would save him, and died there at twenty-five. His [Poems](/book/293?lang=en) and [Endymion](/book/294?lang=en), together with his remarkable letters, made him one of the most loved poets in English.

George Gordon, Lord Byron (1788–1824) was born with a club foot and inherited his title at ten. When the first cantos of [Childe Harold's Pilgrimage](/book/296?lang=en) appeared in 1812 he became the most famous man in England, and after a series of scandals he left the country in 1816, never to return.

In Switzerland and Italy, often in the company of the Shelleys, he wrote his comic masterpiece [Don Juan](/book/295?lang=en). He died of fever in 1824 at Missolonghi, where he had gone to support the Greek war of independence, and he is still honoured in Greece. His daughter Ada Lovelace worked with [Charles Babbage](/author/babbage?lang=en) on the first computer program.

John Milton (1608–1674) was a London scholar-poet who wrote Lycidas and other early poems before devoting twenty years to politics. He wrote pamphlets defending divorce and the freedom of the press, in his famous Areopagitica, and served Cromwell's government as Latin secretary, losing his sight around 1652.

After the monarchy was restored he was briefly imprisoned and lucky to escape execution. Blind, poor and disappointed, he dictated [Paradise Lost](/book/297?lang=en), published in 1667, followed by Paradise Regained and Samson Agonistes. He is often ranked second only to Shakespeare among English poets.

Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) was the son of a London wine merchant and spent his life in royal service: as a page, a soldier captured in France and ransomed with the king's help, a diplomat on missions to Italy and a controller of customs in the port of London.

In his spare time he wrote Troilus and Criseyde and [The Canterbury Tales](/book/298?lang=en), and he was one of the first to make English, rather than French or Latin, the language of serious poetry. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, beginning the tradition of Poets' Corner.

Mary Wollstonecraft (1759–1797) grew up with a violent father and worked as a companion, a schoolmistress and a governess before she made her living as a writer in London. She answered Edmund Burke's attack on the French Revolution with A Vindication of the Rights of Men, and two years later wrote [A Vindication of the Rights of Woman](/book/299?lang=en).

She lived in Paris during the Revolution, travelled in Scandinavia and wrote a fine book of letters about it, and in 1797 married the philosopher William Godwin. She died eleven days after giving birth to their daughter, [Mary Shelley](/author/shelley?lang=en), the future author of Frankenstein.

Daniel Defoe (c. 1660–1731) was the son of a London butcher, became a merchant, went bankrupt more than once and turned to writing pamphlets. In 1703 he was put in the pillory for a satire on religious intolerance, and he later worked as a secret agent for the government in Scotland.

He was nearly sixty when he published [Robinson Crusoe](/book/300?lang=en) in 1719, and in the next few years he wrote [Moll Flanders](/book/301?lang=en) and A Journal of the Plague Year. He wrote hundreds of works in all, and is often called one of the fathers of the English novel.

Jonathan Swift (1667–1745) was born in Dublin after his father's death, studied at Trinity College and worked as secretary to the diplomat Sir William Temple in England. Disappointed in his hopes of advancement, he became Dean of St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin in 1713 and a fierce defender of the Irish against English policy.

His satires, [Gulliver's Travels](/book/302?lang=en) and [A Modest Proposal](/book/303?lang=en) above all, are among the sharpest in any language. He left most of his fortune to found a hospital for the mentally ill, and his epitaph speaks of the savage indignation that tore at his heart.

Charlotte Brontë (1816–1855) grew up in the parsonage at Haworth, on the Yorkshire moors, where she and her brother and sisters invented imaginary kingdoms and wrote tiny books about them. Her two elder sisters died after a harsh boarding school, the model for Lowood in [Jane Eyre](/book/304?lang=en).

After working as a teacher and governess and studying in Brussels, she published poems with her sisters under the names Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell, and in 1847 Jane Eyre made her famous. She outlived all her siblings, married in 1854 and died the following year. Her sister [Emily](/author/ebronte?lang=en) wrote Wuthering Heights.

Emily Brontë (1818–1848) spent almost her whole life at Haworth parsonage on the Yorkshire moors, which she loved and could hardly bear to leave. With her sister Anne she invented the imaginary world of Gondal and wrote poems about it, which Charlotte discovered in 1845 and persuaded her to publish.

Her only novel, [Wuthering Heights](/book/305?lang=en), appeared in 1847 under the name Ellis Bell and puzzled its first readers. She died of tuberculosis a year later, at thirty, refusing a doctor until her last day. Her poems and her novel have made her one of the most original voices in English literature.

Thomas Hardy (1840–1928) was the son of a stonemason in a Dorset hamlet and trained as an architect, restoring country churches. His novels, set in the imaginary region of Wessex, began with modest success, and [Far from the Madding Crowd](/book/307?lang=en) (1874) allowed him to write full time.

After the storm of criticism over [Jude the Obscure](/book/308?lang=en) in 1895 he gave up novels for poetry and wrote some of the best English poems of the twentieth century, many of them about his first wife Emma after her death. His ashes were buried in Westminster Abbey and his heart in his home parish.

Jack London (1876–1916) grew up poor in San Francisco and Oakland and lived a life as wild as his books: an oyster pirate at fifteen, a sailor on a sealing ship to Japan, a tramp, a socialist agitator and a gold seeker in the Klondike in 1897, where he caught scurvy and gathered material for a lifetime.

[The Call of the Wild](/book/309?lang=en) made him famous in 1903, and he became one of the best-paid writers of his day, producing [White Fang](/book/310?lang=en), [The Sea-Wolf](/book/311?lang=en) and [Martin Eden](/book/312?lang=en) among more than fifty books. He died on his California ranch at forty.

Louisa May Alcott (1832–1888) grew up in Concord, Massachusetts, daughter of the idealistic and often penniless educator Bronson Alcott; Emerson and Thoreau were family friends and teachers. To support her family she sewed, taught, worked as a servant and wrote sensational thrillers under a pen name.

During the Civil War she nursed soldiers in Washington until she fell gravely ill. When her publisher asked for a book for girls, she wrote [Little Women](/book/313?lang=en) (1868), drawn from her own family, and it made her famous and secure. She campaigned against slavery and for women's right to vote.

L. Frank Baum (1856–1919) tried many careers before he found his calling: actor, breeder of fancy chickens, shopkeeper and newspaper editor in South Dakota, and travelling salesman. In Chicago he began writing for children, and in 1900, with illustrations by W. W. Denslow, published [The Wonderful Wizard of Oz](/book/314?lang=en).

Its success led to thirteen more Oz books, written partly because children demanded them, and Baum moved to Hollywood, where he even founded a film company. He wanted to write American fairy tales that entertained without frightening children with moral lessons.

Frances Hodgson Burnett (1849–1924) was born in Manchester. After her father's death the family emigrated to Tennessee, where as a teenager she began selling stories to magazines to support them. She became one of the most successful writers of her day, and Little Lord Fauntleroy (1886) started a fashion for velvet suits for boys.

She lived between America and England, and the walled garden of the house she rented in Kent inspired [The Secret Garden](/book/315?lang=en) (1911). Together with [A Little Princess](/book/316?lang=en), it remains one of the best-loved children's books ever written.

Jacob (1785–1863) and Wilhelm Grimm (1786–1859) were brothers from Hanau in Germany who studied law and became librarians and scholars of language. In an age of national awakening, they began collecting folk tales told by friends, relatives and storytellers, publishing the first volume of their Children's and Household Tales in 1812.

They revised the collection through seven editions, and [Grimms' Fairy Tales](/book/317?lang=en) became one of the most read books in the world. They were also great linguists: Jacob described the sound changes of the Germanic languages, and the brothers began the great German dictionary.

Aesop is said to have been a slave on the Greek island of Samos in the sixth century BC who won his freedom through his wit. The historian Herodotus mentions him, and a later popular romance, The Life of Aesop, made him an ugly, clever storyteller who outwitted his masters and died unjustly at Delphi.

Whether or not he wrote them, the short animal fables told under his name, collected in [Aesop's Fables](/book/318?lang=en), have been retold for two and a half thousand years. Their cousin in Arabic literature is [Kalila wa Dimna](/book/1965500?lang=en).

Guy de Maupassant (1850–1893) grew up in Normandy, fought in the Franco-Prussian War and worked as a clerk in Paris ministries while learning to write under the guidance of Gustave Flaubert, an old friend of his mother. [Boule de Suif](/book/320?lang=en), in 1880, made him famous.

In barely ten years he wrote some three hundred short stories and six novels, including [Bel-Ami](/book/319?lang=en), and became the master of the short story in France. He loved rowing on the Seine and the sea, but illness clouded his last years, and he died in a clinic at forty-two.

Honoré de Balzac (1799–1850) was born in Tours, trained as a lawyer and failed as a printer and publisher, leaving debts that pursued him all his life. To pay them he wrote at night, fuelled by enormous quantities of coffee, producing nearly a hundred novels and stories in twenty years.

He gathered them into The Human Comedy, a vast portrait of French society with characters who reappear from book to book; [Eugénie Grandet](/book/323?lang=en) is one of its best-known parts. After eighteen years of letters he married the Polish countess Ewelina Hańska, months before his death.

Gustave Flaubert (1821–1880), the son of a surgeon in Rouen, gave up studying law after a nervous illness and spent most of his life at his family's house at Croisset on the Seine.
