In 1849 he travelled for nearly two years through Egypt and the Middle East, a journey whose colours run through [Salammbô](/book/326?lang=en).

He worked for years on each book, shouting his sentences aloud to test them, in search of the exact word. [Madame Bovary](/book/324?lang=en) brought him a trial and fame, and [Sentimental Education](/book/325?lang=en) followed. He was a mentor to [Maupassant](/author/maupassant?lang=en) and a friend of Turgenev.

Émile Zola (1840–1902) grew up in Aix-en-Provence, where his best friend was the future painter Cézanne, and worked as a clerk for a Paris publisher before becoming a journalist and novelist. He planned and wrote a cycle of twenty novels following one family under the Second Empire, including [Germinal](/book/327?lang=en) and [Nana](/book/328?lang=en).

In 1898 his open letter 'J'accuse...!' defended the wrongly convicted Captain Dreyfus and forced him into exile in England. He died in 1902, poisoned by fumes from a blocked chimney, and his remains were later moved to the Panthéon. [Thérèse Raquin](/book/329?lang=en) was his first success.

Marcel Proust (1871–1922) was born in Paris to a wealthy family, suffered from asthma from childhood and spent his youth in the fashionable salons of Paris society, which he later described with ironic precision. He supported Dreyfus, wrote essays and translated John Ruskin.

After his parents' deaths he withdrew to a cork-lined bedroom and worked through the nights on In Search of Lost Time. Publishers rejected the first volume, [Swann's Way](/book/330?lang=en), and he paid to publish it in 1913; the second volume won the Goncourt Prize in 1919. He died before the last volumes were published.

Nikolai Gogol (1809–1852) was born in the Ukrainian countryside and moved to St Petersburg to make his name, where his comic tales of Ukrainian village life won the friendship of Pushkin. His play The Government Inspector, his story The Overcoat and his novel [Dead Souls](/book/331?lang=en) made him the great satirist of Russian life.

He spent years in Rome, became increasingly religious and tormented, and shortly before his death burned most of the second part of Dead Souls. Later Russian writers, Dostoevsky among them, acknowledged their debt to him; read Dostoevsky's [Poor Folk](/book/19?lang=en) to see it.

Ivan Turgenev (1818–1883) grew up on an estate in central Russia owned by his tyrannical mother, who controlled thousands of serfs. He studied in Berlin, and his [Sportsman's Sketches](/book/335?lang=en), with their sympathetic portraits of serfs, made him famous; an obituary of Gogol earned him a month in detention and exile to his estate.

He spent much of his life abroad, following the singer Pauline Viardot, whom he loved for forty years, and became a friend of Flaubert and a bridge between Russian and Western literature. His novel [Fathers and Sons](/book/334?lang=en) gave the world the word nihilist.

Alexander Pushkin (1799–1837) is Russia's national poet. His great-grandfather, Abram Gannibal, was an African boy taken to Russia who became a favourite of Peter the Great and a general. Pushkin was educated at the imperial lyceum at Tsarskoye Selo and was exiled to the south of Russia for poems against tyranny.

His novel in verse Eugene Onegin, his drama Boris Godunov, his poem The Bronze Horseman and his short stories created modern Russian literature. He died at thirty-seven after a duel with a French officer who had pursued his wife. The library holds his works in Russian, English and Arabic.

Henrik Ibsen (1828–1906) was born in Skien in Norway; his family lost its money when he was a boy, and at fifteen he became a pharmacist's apprentice. He worked in theatres in Bergen and Christiania with little success, and then spent twenty-seven years in Italy and Germany, where he wrote his greatest works.

His verse dramas Brand and [Peer Gynt](/book/341?lang=en) were followed by realistic prose plays about modern life, [A Doll's House](/book/338?lang=en), [Ghosts](/book/340?lang=en) and [Hedda Gabler](/book/339?lang=en), which shocked audiences and changed theatre forever. He is often called the father of modern drama.

Joseph Conrad (1857–1924) was born Józef Korzeniowski to Polish parents in today's Ukraine. His father was exiled for patriotic activities, and Conrad was orphaned at eleven. At sixteen he went to sea from Marseille, and he spent twenty years as a sailor, rising to captain in the British merchant navy.

A voyage up the Congo in 1890 marked him for life and led to [Heart of Darkness](/book/342?lang=en). He began writing in English, his third language, and became one of its great novelists with [Lord Jim](/book/343?lang=en) and [Nostromo](/book/344?lang=en). His books ask what people do when no one is watching.

James Joyce (1882–1941) was born in Dublin, educated by the Jesuits, and left Ireland in 1904 with Nora Barnacle, never to live there again. They lived in Trieste, Zurich and Paris, where he taught English and struggled with poverty and failing eyesight, while writing almost entirely about the city he had left.

[Dubliners](/book/345?lang=en) and [A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man](/book/346?lang=en) were followed by [Ulysses](/book/347?lang=en), published in Paris in 1922 and banned for years in Britain and America, and by the even more experimental Finnegans Wake. He changed what a novel could be.

Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) was the daughter of the critic Leslie Stephen and grew up in a London house full of books. With her sister and friends she formed the circle of artists and writers known as the Bloomsbury Group, and with her husband Leonard she founded the Hogarth Press, which published her own books and those of T. S. Eliot.

Her novels [Mrs Dalloway](/book/348?lang=en), To the Lighthouse and Orlando changed the way fiction follows the mind, and her essay A Room of One's Own argued that a woman needs money and a room of her own to write. She suffered all her life from depression, and drowned herself in 1941.

F. Scott Fitzgerald (1896–1940) was born in St Paul, Minnesota, left Princeton for the army and became famous at twenty-three with his first novel, This Side of Paradise. He married the brilliant Zelda Sayre, named the Jazz Age and lived its glamour in New York and on the French Riviera.

[The Great Gatsby](/book/351?lang=en) (1925), now considered one of the greatest American novels, sold poorly in his lifetime. Zelda's illness, debts and drink darkened his later years, and he died in Hollywood at forty-four, writing film scripts and believing himself a failure.

Henry James (1843–1916) was born in New York, the brother of the philosopher [William James](/author/james?lang=en), and was educated in Europe and America. In 1876 he settled in London, and later in the small town of Rye, and spent his life writing about Americans in Europe and the clash of innocence and experience.

In some twenty novels and more than a hundred stories, including [The Portrait of a Lady](/book/352?lang=en) and [The Turn of the Screw](/book/353?lang=en), he developed a subtle, psychological style that influenced modern fiction. He became a British citizen in 1915, a year before his death.

D. H. Lawrence (1885–1930) was born in a mining town in Nottinghamshire, the son of a coal miner and a former teacher, and trained as a teacher himself. In 1912 he eloped with Frieda Weekley, the German wife of his former professor, and his novel [Sons and Lovers](/book/354?lang=en) (1913), drawn from his own family, made his name.

His next novel, The Rainbow, was banned, and he spent his last years travelling restlessly through Italy, Australia, Mexico and New Mexico, writing novels, poems, travel books and essays and painting. He died of tuberculosis in France at forty-four.

Rudyard Kipling (1865–1936) was born in Bombay, sent to England at five to an unhappy foster home, and returned to India at sixteen to work as a journalist in Lahore. His stories of Anglo-Indian life made him famous in London in his twenties.

[The Jungle Book](/book/355?lang=en), written in Vermont, [Kim](/book/356?lang=en) and [Just So Stories](/book/357?lang=en) became classics, and in 1907 he became the first English-language writer to win the Nobel Prize. His poem 'If—' is still widely quoted, though his support for empire makes him a controversial figure today. His only son was killed in the First World War.

Rabindranath Tagore (1861–1941) was born in Calcutta, the youngest son of a great Bengali family of reformers and artists. He wrote poems, stories, novels, plays and some two thousand songs, and his songs became the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh.

He founded a school in the countryside at Santiniketan, which grew into a university, and in 1913 became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize, for [Gitanjali](/book/358?lang=en). In 1919 he returned his British knighthood in protest at the massacre at Amritsar. [The Home and the World](/book/359?lang=en) and [The Post Office](/book/360?lang=en) show his range.

Hippocrates (c. 460–370 BC) was a physician from the Greek island of Kos who taught that diseases have natural causes, not divine ones, and that doctors should observe their patients carefully and record what they see. Little is known of his life, and the collection of some sixty medical texts that bears his name was written by many authors.

The Hippocratic writings include the famous Oath and the aphorism 'Life is short, the art is long'. Known in Arabic as Buqrat, Hippocrates was translated by Hunayn ibn Ishaq and his school, and his ideas shaped medicine in the Islamic world and Europe for two thousand years.

William Harvey (1578–1657) studied medicine at Cambridge and at Padua, the leading medical school of Europe, and became physician to Kings James I and Charles I. Through years of careful dissections and experiments on animals, he showed that the heart pumps the blood in a continuous circle through the body.

His short book On the Motion of the Heart and Blood (1628) overturned theories that had stood since antiquity, and it is in the library in English translation. Four centuries earlier, the Arab physician Ibn al-Nafis had already described how blood passes through the lungs, a discovery that Europe learned of much later.

Henry Gray (1827–1861) was a young anatomist and surgeon at St George's Hospital in London. With his colleague Henry Vandyke Carter, who drew the illustrations from their own dissections, he produced Anatomy, Descriptive and Surgical in 1858, a clear and practical textbook for medical students.

Gray died of smallpox at thirty-four, caught while nursing his nephew, only three years after the book appeared. Revised many times, Gray's Anatomy is still in print more than a century and a half later, one of the most famous medical books ever written.

Florence Nightingale (1820–1910) was named after Florence, the city where she was born. Her wealthy family opposed her wish to become a nurse, but she trained in Germany, and in 1854 led a team of nurses to the British military hospital at Scutari during the Crimean War, where soldiers called her the Lady with the Lamp.

Back in England she used statistics, and diagrams she designed, to prove that most soldiers died of disease, not wounds, and to reform hospitals and sanitation. She founded a school of nursing at St Thomas' Hospital and wrote [Notes on Nursing](/book/367?lang=en). She was the first woman to receive the Order of Merit.

Euclid lived in Alexandria around 300 BC, under the first Ptolemy, and almost nothing else is known of him. He is said to have told the king who wanted an easier way to learn mathematics that there is no royal road to geometry.

His Elements, thirteen books on geometry and numbers built from a few definitions and axioms, has been taught for more than two thousand years. It was translated into Arabic in the age of the Abbasids, studied and improved by Arab mathematicians, and first reached Latin Europe through a translation from the Arabic.

Galileo Galilei (1564–1642) was born in Pisa and taught mathematics there and at Padua. He studied falling bodies and pendulums, and in 1609 built a telescope with which he discovered the moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus and the mountains of the Moon, which he announced in The Sidereal Messenger.

His defence of the idea that the Earth moves around the Sun brought him before the Inquisition in 1633; forced to recant, he spent his last years under house arrest near Florence, where, going blind, he completed his book on motion that prepared the way for [Newton](/author/newton?lang=en).

Nicolaus Copernicus (1473–1543) was born in Toruń in Poland, studied in Kraków and in Italy, at Bologna, Padua and Ferrara, and spent most of his life as a canon of Frombork cathedral, working as an administrator and physician while observing the sky.

His book On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, published in the year of his death, placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the centre of the universe. Historians have shown that he used mathematical models developed earlier by astronomers of the Islamic world, at the observatory of Maragha. [Galileo](/author/galileo?lang=en) took up his cause.

James Clerk Maxwell (1831–1879) was born in Edinburgh and published his first scientific paper at fourteen. He explained the rings of Saturn, produced the first colour photograph and helped found the theory of gases, but his greatest achievement was a set of equations uniting electricity, magnetism and light.

He predicted that light is an electromagnetic wave, opening the way to radio and the physics of the twentieth century; Einstein kept his portrait on his study wall. He became the first director of the Cavendish Laboratory at Cambridge and died at forty-eight.

Michael Faraday (1791–1867) was the son of a London blacksmith and left school early to become a bookbinder's apprentice, educating himself by reading the books he bound. After attending lectures by the chemist Humphry Davy, he sent Davy his notes and was taken on as his assistant at the Royal Institution.

He discovered electromagnetic induction, the principle of the electric generator, and laid the foundations of electrochemistry, as recorded in his [Experimental Researches in Electricity](/book/375?lang=en). He started the Royal Institution's Christmas lectures for young people, among them [The Chemical History of a Candle](/book/374?lang=en), and refused a knighthood.

Nikola Tesla (1856–1943) was born to a Serbian family in a village in today's Croatia, studied engineering in Graz and emigrated to America in 1884, where he worked briefly for Thomas Edison. His alternating-current motor and power system, backed by George Westinghouse, won the battle of the currents against Edison's direct current.

He experimented with wireless power, radio and high-voltage electricity, and dreamed of a worldwide wireless network, but died poor in a New York hotel. The unit of magnetic field is named after him, and the library holds his lectures on alternating currents.

Charles Babbage (1791–1871) was a Cambridge mathematician, Lucasian professor like Newton before him, who grew frustrated with the errors in printed mathematical tables and set out to build a machine to calculate them. His Difference Engine, and then his more ambitious Analytical Engine, programmed with punched cards, anticipated the computer by a century.

Neither was finished in his lifetime, but Ada Lovelace, daughter of [Lord Byron](/author/byron?lang=en), wrote notes on the Analytical Engine that included the first published computer program. He also wrote on industry in [On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures](/book/378?lang=en) and told his own story in [Passages from the Life of a Philosopher](/book/377?lang=en).

Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BC) was a Roman architect and military engineer who built siege machines for Julius Caesar's armies. In later life, with a pension from the emperor Augustus, he wrote a treatise on everything he knew about building, the only complete work on architecture to survive from antiquity.

[The Ten Books on Architecture](/book/379?lang=en) cover materials, temples, houses, water, machines and city planning, and teach that good buildings must be strong, useful and beautiful. Rediscovered in the fifteenth century, the book shaped Renaissance architecture and inspired [Leonardo da Vinci](/author/vinci?lang=en).

Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), born Georg Bauer in Saxony, was a scholar and physician who worked in the mining towns of Bohemia and Saxony. Instead of dismissing mining as work for the uneducated, he spent years studying the miners, their tools, machines and methods, and the minerals they dug.

His great book De Re Metallica, published in 1556, with nearly three hundred woodcuts, was the standard work on mining and metallurgy for two centuries; in 1912 it was translated into English by Herbert Hoover, the future American president, and his wife Lou. He is often called the father of mineralogy.

Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519) was born near the town of Vinci, the illegitimate son of a Florentine notary, and trained in the workshop of the painter Verrocchio. He worked for the rulers of Florence and Milan, where he painted The Last Supper, and spent his last years in France as the guest of King Francis I.

His paintings, among them the Mona Lisa, are few, but his notebooks are full of studies of anatomy, flight, water, optics and machines, written in mirror script. [The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci](/book/381?lang=en) let us follow his endless curiosity; for one of his sources, see [Vitruvius](/book/379?lang=en).

Edwin A. Abbott (1838–1926) became headmaster of the City of London School at twenty-six and led it for nearly twenty-five years, while writing books on English grammar, on Shakespeare's language, on how to write clearly and on theology.

He is remembered today for one small book, [Flatland](/book/382?lang=en), published in 1884 under the pen name A Square: a mathematical fantasy about a two-dimensional world that is also a satire of Victorian society. Mathematicians still recommend it as an introduction to the idea of other dimensions.

William James (1842–1910), the older brother of the novelist [Henry James](/author/jamesh?lang=en), studied painting and then medicine, and after years of depression became a professor at Harvard, where he taught the first course in psychology in America and set up one of the first psychology laboratories.

His [Principles of Psychology](/book/383?lang=en) made the new science readable, his [Varieties of Religious Experience](/book/384?lang=en) studied faith with sympathy, and his philosophy of pragmatism asked what difference an idea makes in practice. He wrote with a warmth and clarity rare among philosophers.

Gustave Le Bon (1841–1931) was a French physician who became a traveller, anthropologist and popular writer on society and psychology. He journeyed through North Africa, the Middle East and India, and his book The Civilisation of the Arabs (1884) admired the achievements of Arab science and culture at a time when such views were rare in Europe; translated by Adel Zuaiter, it became a classic in Arabic.

His most influential book, [The Crowd](/book/745?lang=en) (1895), argued that people in a crowd lose their individual judgement, and was read by Freud as well as by politicians of every kind. The library holds several of his works in Arabic translation.

Thorstein Veblen (1857–1929) was born in Wisconsin to Norwegian immigrant farmers, earned a doctorate in philosophy at Yale and then, unable to find work, spent seven years on his family's farm reading. At the University of Chicago he published [The Theory of the Leisure Class](/book/386?lang=en) (1899), which made him famous.

An eccentric teacher and a sharp, ironic writer, he moved from university to university and spent his career criticising business culture and wasteful consumption. He died in August 1929, a few months before the stock market crash that seemed to prove him right.
